Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c2120206baad35af57fdc2f467b72161]

Content:
First, note that the ratio of the smaller area to the larger area is

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{4\,\textrm{cm}^2}{24\,\textrm{cm}^2} = \dfrac{1}{6}.]

Content:
Therefore, the shaded area is precisely one-sixth of the total area.

Graphic:

Consequently, [MATH: \angle AOB] represents [MATH: \dfrac16] of a complete turn. So, the measure of [MATH: \angle{AOB}] is

Content:
[MATH: m∠AOB|= (1)/(6) ⋅ 360^{∘} = 60^{∘}.]

sections.normalized_html:
From the diagram, we have that the radius [MATH: r] of the circle is [MATH: 4\,\textrm{cm}.]

Now, [MATH: \angle{AOB}] is the central angle that intercepts the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}.] So the measure of the major arc (that corresponds to our sector) is [MATH: 360^\circ - m\angle{AOB} = 360^\circ - 30^\circ = 330^\circ.]

Note that the ratio of the measure of the major arc to a full circle turn is [MATH: \dfrac{330^\circ}{360^\circ} = \dfrac{11}{12}.]

Therefore, if the area of the circle is [MATH: \mathcal{A}], then the area of the major sector will be

[MATH: (11)/(12) ⋅ A|= (11)/(12) ⋅ πr^{2}; = (11)/(12) ⋅ π ⋅ 4^{2}; = (44π)/(3)cm^{2}.]

[MATH: 9π|= (1)/(4) ⋅ πr^{2}; 9π|= (1)/(4) ⋅ πr^{2}; 9|= (1)/(4) ⋅ r^{2}; r|= ± 6]

Therefore, [MATH: r=6\,\textrm{km}], since a distance can't be negative.
